_meta.description: Typical UMF limit ranges for functional glossy glazes, as heuristics for flagging a recipe that's likely to craze, be under-durable, or misbehave. These are GUIDANCE from common ceramics references (e.g. Hesselberth & Roy 'Mastering Cone 6 Glazes' for the cone-6 set), not hard rules — plenty of good glazes sit outside them. Values are UMF (fluxes = 1.0). ratios are molar.
_meta.source: Compiled from common glaze-chemistry references. Approximate.
_meta.targets: Pick the target that matches what the glaze is TRYING to be. Checking a shino or a tenmoku against cone6-glossy produces a wall of flags that are the glaze's signature rather than its faults — see `families` below.
_meta.version_note: 0.2.0 adds cone6-iron-crystal, cone6-copper-red and cone6-matte, plus the `families` block describing glaze types that sit outside the glossy limits by design.

cone6-iron-crystal.label: Cone 6 iron crystallisation (kaki / tenmoku / oil spot / teadust)
notes: Low alumina is the point: alumina raises melt viscosity and suppresses nucleation, so the glossy limits' 0.25-0.5 band actively prevents the effect.
B₂O₃ near zero — boron suppresses iron devitrification.

MgO near zero, and this is the one that most often silently kills the effect: Fe²⁺ and Mg²⁺ substitute nearly freely (same charge, near-identical ionic radius, both octahedral), so iron dissolves into the Mg-silicate structure instead of precipitating its own phase.

Iron loading is an ADDITION, not part of this UMF: 11-14% for kaki. 20% overshoots and tends to crawl — that is a dried-layer failure (iron is a non-plastic filler with high water demand, so the raw layer has almost no clay bond), not a melt failure.
Phosphorus helps: 2-6% bone ash or TCP drives the liquid-liquid phase separation that seeds hematite.
Needs a slow cool specifically through 1050-900 °C, not merely a slow drop below peak. This conflicts with inclusion stains, which want a fast drop from peak — fire them in separate loads.

cone6-copper-red.label: Cone 6 copper red via in-glaze SiC reduction (electric)
notes: A glassy oxblood is properly cone 9-10 reduction; at cone 6 in an electric kiln the route is in-glaze reduction with silicon carbide, not atmosphere.
High alumina keeps copper ionic and green — hence the tight low band.
Excess boron fights the red and raises expansion.

Additions, outside this UMF: CuO 0.3-0.5%, SnO₂ ~1% to nucleate colloidal copper, SiC 0.25-0.3% at 500 mesh or 0.5-0.75% at 800 mesh. Finer mesh is better — faster complete oxidation, earlier gas release, no lizard-skin texture.
2% SiC is 4-8× the published range and gives a foamed grey, with LOI more than doubling and the gas arriving late while the melt is sealing.
Prefer a known-style recipe that has actually produced red in someone's electric kiln over a theoretically perfect computed one; tune expansion after you have a tile that reds up.

cone6-matte.label: Cone 6 matte (dolomite / calcium-magnesium silicate matte)
notes: A true matte is a crystallised surface, not an underfired one. If it's dry and pinholed rather than smooth and buttery, it's underfired — a different problem with a different fix.
'Dolomite matte' names the INPUT; 'diopside matte' names the OUTPUT crystal (CaMgSi₂O₆). Same phenomenon described from two ends — people use them interchangeably and mean the same glaze.

Magnesia matte is genuinely distinct: high MgO with low CaO, usually from talc, giving enstatite/forsterite rather than diopside. Drier, more opaque, more likely to be the surface people call 'satin'.

Matte surfaces are more leachable than glossy ones at the same chemistry — the crystallised surface has more area and the residual glass between crystals is alkali-enriched. Be conservative about matte interiors on functional ware.

families._note: Glaze families that sit OUTSIDE the functional-glossy limits by design. When a recipe flags heavily against cone6-glossy, check this list before calling it broken — the flags may be the signature. Say which family it looks like and what the flags mean, rather than reciting them as faults.

shino.signature: High Al₂O₃ (0.8-1.1), high KNaO (0.6-0.8), low Si:Al (3.5-4.5), low CaO, low-to-no B₂O₃.
shino.reading: Every one of those is the shino. A cone 6 soda-ash shino flags five ways against cone6-glossy and is working exactly as intended; the classic Malcolm Davis cone 10 shino computes further outside still (Si:Al 3.49, Al₂O₃ 1.093, KNaO 0.77). Do not 'correct' it toward the glossy limits.

iron-crystal.signature: Low Al₂O₃ (0.2-0.3), high Si:Al (10-14), B₂O₃ and MgO near zero.
iron-crystal.reading: Use target cone6-iron-crystal. Against the glossy limits the low alumina reads as 'runny and under-durable', which for a tenmoku or kaki is the operating point.

crystalline.signature: Very low Al₂O₃ (often <0.15), very high Si:Al, high ZnO or TiO₂, extremely fluid.
crystalline.reading: Macro-crystalline glazes need a melt fluid enough to run off the pot — hence catchers. Durability and running flags are expected, not faults.

matte.signature: Low Si:Al (4-6.5), higher alumina and/or high CaO+MgO.
matte.reading: Use target cone6-matte. Distinguish a crystallised matte from an underfired one before diagnosing.

raku.signature: Very high alkali, very low alumina and silica, high expansion.
raku.reading: Crazing is the intended decorative effect and the ware is non-functional. Expansion flags are meaningless here.

notes.SiO2_Al2O3: Lower ratio (~5-7) tends matte/silky; higher (~8-12) glossier/glassier. Very high with low alumina risks running and low durability.
notes.Al2O3: Too low → runny, soft, less durable. High alumina (>~0.5 with lower silica) → alumina matte.
notes.B2O3: A melter that also lowers thermal expansion. Useful to fix crazing without adding high-expansion alkalis.
notes.crazing: Glaze contracts more than the clay body on cooling → cracks. Lower expansion: cut KNaO (Na2O worst), add SiO2, add B2O3, swap some flux to MgO or Li2O.
notes.shivering: Glaze contracts less than body → flakes off edges. Raise expansion: more KNaO, less SiO2/B2O3.
notes.durability: Very high alkali (KNaO) with low SiO2/Al2O3 leaches — avoid for food surfaces. Keep silica and alumina toward the upper end for functional ware.
